summary: Extends the postmaster concept to X.400 mail domains that have registered RFC 1327 mapping rules and therefore appear to have normal RFC 822-style addresses. It was proposed as a standard. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Every mail office should have a person you can write to for help. This extends that idea to an older mail system.

questions: how to support postmaster in x.400
subtitle: A convention for supporting the postmaster address in X.400 mail domains mapped to RFC 822.

tldr.problem: X.400 mail domains mapped to RFC 822 addresses using RFC 1327 rules appear as normal Internet email addresses, but many do not support the postmaster address required by RFC 822 and RFC 1123.
tldr.mechanism: This standard requires that if any valid address exists in the form 'user@domain', the address 'postmaster@domain' must also be valid, with mail routed to a responsible party for the site.
tldr.outcome: This ensures seamless integration of X.400 and RFC 822 mail systems but requires X.400 software to support forwarding or aliasing for the postmaster mailbox.

today: RFC 1648 is Historic. X.400 has largely been replaced by SMTP and other Internet mail systems, making this convention obsolete. Modern mail systems are almost exclusively SMTP-based.

sections.title: The Postmaster Requirement
sections.content: RFC 822 and the Internet Host Requirements (RFC 1123) require that every Internet host support the email address postmaster so that mail administrators and system operators can contact a responsible person without knowing a specific user name. This is essential for coordinating mail system operation across many sites and networks.
sections.eli5: The Internet requires that you can always send mail to 'postmaster' at any domain to report problems.

sections.title: The X.400 Mapping Problem
sections.content: Some Internet sites use the X.400 email protocol. RFC 1327 defines how to map X.400 addresses to and from RFC 822 format. When mapping rules are registered, X.400 users appear to have normal RFC 822-style email addresses. However, many X.400 systems do not support the postmaster address even though the domains appear as standard RFC 822 addresses. This breaks expectations and prevents mail administrators from contacting responsible parties at those domains.
sections.eli5: X.400 is an older mail system that looks like Internet mail when you map its addresses, but it does not have a postmaster mailbox.

sections.title: Mandatory Postmaster Support
sections.content: This convention requires that for every X.400 domain with registered RFC 1327 mapping rules, if any address of the form user@domain is valid, then postmaster@domain must also be valid. X.400(1988) systems should also support CommonName=Postmaster. Mail software that cannot natively support this should be upgraded. If that is not possible, workarounds include creating a mailing list for postmaster or using X.400 autoforwarding features to route postmaster mail to a central mailbox.
sections.eli5: X.400 systems that look like Internet mail must accept postmaster messages, either through built-in support or by forwarding them somewhere.
